files.lesson.md: --- order: 42 unit: composite10 node: [AC9M10M01 n3, AC9M10M01 n4] uses: [AC9M10M01 n1, AC9M10M01 n2, AC9M9M01 n2] assumes: [AC9M10M01 n1] connection: rainwater-tank title: Volume of composite objects summary: "Find a composite volume by adding parts or taking one away, in whichever way is easier, then say what the model assumes. A rainwater tank, a pool with a deep end and a silo." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "How much rain does it take to fill a water tank?" --- Rain falling on a roof runs into a tank. The Bureau of Meteorology says each millimetre of rain on each square metre gives about a litre ([Bureau of Meteorology](https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/how/faq-data.shtml), checked 25 October 2026). This tank is a cylinder with a cone-shaped bottom, and a roof of 100 m² feeds it (shape and sizes made up for the task). How many millimetres of rain fill it from empty? Have a guess, and we'll come back to it at the end. ## Predict: filling the tank ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to the rainfall shows who leaves the cone out, who counts it as a full cylinder, and who loses a factor of 1000 between cubic metres and litres." check: type: predict q: "The tank is a cylinder (radius 1.1 m, wall height 2 m) with a cone-shaped bottom 0.6 m deep. A roof of 100 m² feeds it. About how many millimetres of rain fill the empty tank?" options: - "About 84 mm" - "About 76 mm" - "About 99 mm" - "About 8 mm" actual: "About 84 mm. The tank holds about 8.36 m³, which is 8360 litres. Each millimetre on 100 m² gives 100 litres, so 8360 ÷ 100 is about 84 mm. Leaving out the cone gives 76 mm, and counting it as a full cylinder gives 99 mm." ``` The picture isn't to scale. What is the tank's capacity in litres? ## Run: the cone at the bottom ```step stage: run insight: "The cone-shaped bottom is one third of base area times depth, and it is added to the cylinder above it." check: { type: number, q: "The cone's base is the circle of area $3.8$ m² and it is $0.6$ m deep. What is its volume? (m³, 2 decimal places)", answer: 0.76, tolerance: 0.02, explain: "One third of 3.8 × 0.6 = 0.76 m³." } ``` Remember from the silo: a cone holds a third of the cylinder that fits round it. The cylinder part of the tank is the base area $3.8$ m² times $2$ m. ## Investigate: add, or take away ```step stage: investigate insight: "A composite volume is found by adding parts or by taking a part away from a bigger solid, and both give the same answer. A hole is always taken away. Tom adds the hole." tasks: - hint: ["Cylinder: base area 3.8 times 2 is 7.6.", "Then add the cone, 0.76."] check: { type: number, q: "What is the tank's total volume? (m³, 2 decimal places)", answer: 8.36, tolerance: 0.02, explain: "Cylinder 3.8 × 2 = 7.6 (more exactly 7.599), cone 0.76. Total 8.36 m³." } smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is $7.6 + 0.76$?", answer: 8.36, tolerance: 0.005, explain: "7.6 + 0.76 = 8.36." } - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#tom" text: "Tom finds the volume of concrete in a block with a hole through it. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: hole-added explain: "Line 4: a hole has no concrete in it. Tom added the hole's 1570 cm³ instead of taking it away." - check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A pool is 12 m long and 6 m wide. The first 8 m is 1 m deep and the last 4 m is 2.5 m deep (made up for the task). What is its volume? (m³) Find it by adding two boxes, then check it by taking one box away from a bigger one." steps: - ["$V = 8 \\times 6 \\times 1 + 4 \\times 6 \\times 2.5$", "add: a shallow box and a deep box"] - ["$V = 48 + 60 = 108$", "the total"] - ["$12 \\times 6 \\times 2.5 - 8 \\times 6 \\times 1.5 = 180 - 72 = 108$", "check: a big box as deep as the deep end, minus the missing water"] answer: "108" answerLabel: "Volume (m³)" feedback: - ["180", "That is the whole pool as deep as the deep end. Take the missing water away."] - ["48", "That is only the shallow part. The deep part holds water too."] criteria: - "I found the volume by adding two boxes." - "I checked it by taking a box away from a bigger one." - "Both ways gave the same number." explain: "Adding: 48 + 60 = 108 m³. Taking away: 180 − 72 = 108 m³. The same, so I can trust it." ``` ### The whole tank Add the cylinder and the cone, and keep the units in cubic metres. ### Find the mistake Read Tom's working. A concrete block has a round hole drilled right through it. ### Two ways to see a pool A pool is 10 m long and 5 m wide. The first 6 m is 1 m deep and the last 4 m is 2 m deep (made up for the task). ```worked V = 6 \times 5 \times 1 + 4 \times 5 \times 2 :: Add: the shallow part is one box and the deep part is another. V = 30 + 40 = 70 \text{ m}^3 :: The total. V = 10 \times 5 \times 2 - 6 \times 5 \times 1 :: Take away: a big box as deep as the deep end, minus the box of missing water. V = 100 - 30 = 70 \text{ m}^3 :: The same answer both ways. ``` Now try a bigger pool on paper: work it both ways, one step per line, then type the volume. ## Modify: change one thing ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a part-filled silo, a bigger roof for the tank, and a silo filled exactly to the join." tasks: - hint: ["Grain only fills the cylinder, up to 4 m.", "Base area times 4."] check: { type: number, q: "The silo (radius $2$ m, wall $6$ m tall, cone roof) is filled with grain to $4$ m up the wall. How many cubic metres of grain? (1 decimal place, $\\pi \\approx 3.14$)", answer: 50.2, tolerance: 0.2, explain: "3.14 × 2² × 4 = 50.24 m³. The cone is empty." } - hint: ["The tank holds about 8360 litres.", "1 mm on 120 m² is 120 litres."] check: { type: number, q: "A different roof is $120$ m². The tank holds $8360$ litres. How many millimetres of rain fill it? (1 decimal place)", answer: 69.7, tolerance: 0.2, explain: "1 mm on 120 m² is 120 litres, so 8360 ÷ 120 = 69.7 mm." } - hint: ["Which solid is left to fill?", "A third of the cylinder that fits round the roof."] check: { type: number, q: "Edge case: the silo is filled exactly up to the join, where the cone starts. How many cubic metres of room are left in the roof? (1 decimal place, $\\pi \\approx 3.14$)", answer: 6.3, tolerance: 0.05, explain: "The roof cone is ⅓ × 3.14 × 2² × 1.5 = 6.28 m³." } ``` ### Half-full silo ### A bigger roof ### Filled to the join ## Practise: composite volumes ```step stage: practise insight: "Adding blocks, taking a hole away, and the review of percentage error." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A step: a block $3$ m long, $2$ m wide and $1$ m tall sits on a block $5$ m long, $2$ m wide and $0.5$ m tall. What is the total volume? (m³)" answer: 11 explain: "3 × 2 × 1 = 6 and 5 × 2 × 0.5 = 5. Total 11 m³." - hint: ["Whole cylinder minus the hole.", "The hole's radius is 0.25 m."] check: type: number q: "A concrete pipe is $4$ m long, with an outer radius of $0.3$ m and a hole radius of $0.25$ m. What is the volume of concrete? (m³, 2 decimal places, $\\pi \\approx 3.14$)" answer: 0.35 tolerance: 0.01 explain: "3.14 × 0.3² × 4 = 1.1304 and 3.14 × 0.25² × 4 = 0.785. The difference is 0.3454, about 0.35 m³." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is the volume of the whole outer cylinder, as if it were solid? (m³, 2 decimal places)", answer: 1.13, tolerance: 0.01, explain: "3.14 × 0.3² × 4 = 1.1304." } - check: type: number q: "Review: a student works out the tank's volume as $8.4$ m³ when the true value is $8.36$ m³. What is the percentage error? (%, 1 decimal place)" answer: 0.5 tolerance: 0.05 explain: "The absolute error is 0.04 m³. 0.04 ÷ 8.36 × 100 = 0.48%, about 0.5%." ``` ### Steps ### The pipe ### Review ## Make: the tank, and what it assumes ```step stage: make insight: "A model is only as good as its assumptions. Write them down, calculate, then say which way each one pushes the answer." tasks: - hint: ["Assumptions first: shape, walls, and the rain.", "1 mm on 100 m² is 100 litres."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Use the tank (radius 1.1 m, wall height 2 m, cone bottom 0.6 m deep) and the 100 m² roof. How many millimetres of rain fill it from empty? On paper, write down at least three assumptions first, then your steps. (1 decimal place, $\\pi \\approx 3.14$)" steps: - ["Assume: a perfect cylinder and a perfect cone, walls with no thickness, filled to the brim, and every drop that lands on the roof reaches the tank.", "the model's assumptions"] - ["$V = 7.6 + 0.76 = 8.36 \\text{ m}^3 = 8360 \\text{ L}$", "the capacity in litres"] - ["$1 \\text{ mm on } 100 \\text{ m}^2 = 100 \\text{ L}$", "the Bureau's rule"] - ["$8360 \\div 100 = 83.6$", "the rain in millimetres"] answer: "83.6" answerLabel: "Rain (mm)" tolerance: 0.5 feedback: - ["76", "That leaves the cone out. The cone holds water too."] - ["98.8", "That treats the cone as a full cylinder. It holds a third of that."] - ["836", "1 mm on 100 m² is 100 litres, so divide the litres by 100."] criteria: - "I wrote at least three assumptions before calculating." - "I added the cone to the cylinder." - "I changed cubic metres to litres before using the Bureau's rule." explain: "8360 litres ÷ 100 litres per millimetre is about 83.6 mm, if the model's assumptions hold." - check: type: question q: "A model treats the silo as a perfect cylinder topped by a perfect cone, filled to the very tip, and gets $81.6$ m³. Which assumption most likely makes this too big?" options: - "Grain doesn't fill the very tip of the cone, so the real amount is a bit less" - "A cone holds a third of its cylinder, so the model has left out two thirds" - "Grain is measured in cubic metres, which is too small a unit" - "Nothing: a model is an exact copy of the silo" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "A third is correct for a cone. The model has used it properly." - "The unit is not an assumption: cubic metres are fine." - "A model simplifies the silo. That is why it needs assumptions." explain: "Grain doesn't pile into the very tip of the roof, and the walls are not perfect, so 81.6 m³ is the most the silo could hold." - check: type: question q: "The Bureau's rule of 1 litre for each millimetre on each square metre is approximate. Some rain is lost from a real roof. Compared with 83.6 mm, how much rain must really fall to fill the tank?" options: - "More, because some of the rain never reaches the tank" - "Less, because the tank is a cone" - "The same, because the model is exact" - "It can't be estimated" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "The cone is already in the 8360 litres." - "The Bureau calls its rule approximate." - "It can be estimated: the real amount is somewhat more." explain: "If some rain is lost, more has to fall for 8360 litres to arrive." ``` ### The tank, on paper Back to the tank. Write your assumptions first, work it out on paper, then type your answer. ### The silo's assumptions ### Rain that is lost **Also used in** - **Pools and construction.** A pool with a deep end, a step, a dam wall: boxes and prisms added or taken away. - **Tanks and silos.** Capacity questions always start with the shape, then the assumptions. - **Measurement error.** How far out an answer could be when the sizes are only measured to the nearest unit. ```teacher summary: Students find the volume of composite objects by adding parts or taking one away, check by a second route, then state what a model of a tank or silo assumes (AC9M10M01, nodes 3 and 4). time: 50 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 17 min goals: - I can find a composite volume by adding or by taking away. - I can check by finding it a second way. - I can say what a model of a tank or silo assumes. struggle: "Adding a hole, and treating the model's answer as exact. Ask: is there anything in a hole? What did the model leave out?" before: > Students need Break it into solids and Surface area of composite objects. Two ideas: the same volume can be found by adding parts or by subtracting one from a bigger solid (the pool), and a model's answer is only as good as its assumptions (Make, which is the modelling task of node 4). 1 mm of rain on 1 m² of surface is about 1 litre (Bureau of Meteorology, approximate). The tank's cone-shaped bottom, the roof, the pool and the silo are made up for the task. Real tank and silo brochures make a good extension: the brochure's stated capacity is the check. The Make asks students to write at least three assumptions on paper before calculating. Typical ones: perfect shapes, no wall thickness, filled to the brim, all the rain reaches the tank, grain fills the cone's tip. The silo question uses the 81.6 m³ answer from Break it into solids. running: - "Predict: show of hands before the check. Those who chose 76 left the cone out; 99 counted it as a full cylinder." - "Paper: the pool in Investigate and the tank in Make are worked on paper first. Books out; in Make, assumptions come first." - "Make: ask which assumption they think changes the answer most, and which way." stuck: - see: A student gets 17 570 cm³ for the block with the hole. ask: Is there concrete in the hole? fix: No. Take the hole's volume away from the block. - see: A student gets 836 mm. ask: How many litres is 1 mm on 100 m²? fix: 100 litres. Divide 8360 by 100. - see: A student says the model is wrong because the silo has walls. ask: What would you change in the model, and which way would the answer move? fix: Thicker walls make the inside smaller, so the model's volume is a little too big. stretch: Add a wall thickness of 2 cm to the tank and work out the inside radius. How much does the capacity change, as a percentage? support: "A printed pool and tank with the boxes and cone drawn separately, and a frame: assumption, calculation, which way it pushes." leads: | Finishes AC9M10M01 (nodes 3 and 4). Where it leads: Year 10 measurement error, and modelling in Functions. exit: q: A pool has a shallow end and a deep end. Name two ways to find its volume. a: Add the shallow box and the deep box, or take the missing water away from a box as deep as the deep end. explain: > A composite volume is found by adding the parts or by taking a part away from a bigger solid. Both ways give the same answer, so one checks the other. A model of a real tank or silo makes assumptions, such as perfect shapes, and its answer is only as good as they are. sources: - title: Climate data FAQ (Bureau of Meteorology) url: https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/how/faq-data.shtml checked: 2026-10-25 ```

# Tom's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: tom
A concrete block is 40 cm by 20 cm by 20 cm. A round hole with a radius of 5 cm goes straight through the 20 cm height.
Block: 40 × 20 × 20 = 16 000 cm³.
Hole: 3.14 × 5² × 20 = 1570 cm³.
Concrete: 16 000 + 1570 = 17 570 cm³.
# endregion
